name: Otuho
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Coates, Heather. 1985. Otuho phonology and orthography. In Mary Ruth Wise & Richard L. Watson (eds.), Occasional Papers in the Study of Sudanese Languages 4, 86-118. Juba: Summer Institute of Linguistics / Institute of Regional Languages.
catalog_locator: Sec. 2.4 'Stress and Tone', p. 102 (header '102 COATES'; p. 109 of the 2005 facsimile)
catalog_quote: Stress in Otuho is very indistinct, and many words do not have a stressed syllable. A strong consonant often gives greater stress to the syllable in which it occurs. A neutral consonant may be strongly articulated when the word in which it occurs is being emphasised, producing the same phonetic result as a strong consonant, i.e. a stressed syllable. Muratori gives an example of what he claims to be a stress contrast, but on further investigation it would seem that tone is the most significant feature in the contrast and that stress is not phonemic. ... Tone, on the other hand, is phonemic, and has both lexical and grammatical functions. A full investigation and analysis has not yet been completed, but some examples are given below of tone contrasts in identical or analogous environments. There are three or four level tones, and several glides which may be either rising or falling.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File check: (159 pp, image-only I.R.I.S. facsimile, SIL Internet Archive copy) is held by the project with and the per-page scanned. I rendered p. 109 (printed p. 102, header '102 COATES') at 120 dpi and read it directly: below Chart 4 (Consonants: strong t k d r w: l: y: s n: / weak / neutral) and Chart 5 (Vowels) is the heading '2.4. Stress and Tone' followed by exactly the reported prose: 'Stress in Otuho is very indistinct, and many words do not have a stressed syllable. A strong consonant often gives greater stress to the syllable in which it occurs. A neutral consonant may be strongly articulated when the word in which it occurs is being emphasised, producing the same phonetic result…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Otuho has no phonemic and no positionally fixed word stress: perceived syllable prominence is weak, often absent, and where present is a by-product of a fortis ('strong') onset consonant (t:, d:, k, n:, l:, r etc.) or of emphatic articulation; apparent stress minimal pairs (Muratori's ojó/ójo) are tone contrasts. Tone (three or four levels plus rising/falling glides) is lexically and grammatically contrastive.
new_statements.exceptions: None as such; Coates reanalyses Muratori's (1938: 18) claimed accent pair 'ojo 'said' vs o'jo 'with' as tonal. Muratori 1938 (sec. 433-437, pp. 203-204) separately gives construction-specific 'accento tonico' positions for imperative persons (2sg penultimate, monosyllabic roots final, 3pl final) while conceding tone matters more than accent.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement based on isolated words/short phrases from fieldwork in Torit 1983-85; emphasis (phrase-level) can strengthen a neutral consonant and yield a 'stressed' syllable. Tone analysis explicitly preliminary.
new_statements.identity_note: Coates 1985 describes Otuho as spoken around Torit (SIL fieldwork 1983-85), i.e. Otuho proper = otuh1238 / ISO lot; Muratori 1938 and Raglan 1922 describe the same language under the names Lotuxo / Lotuko (Torit-area 'Lotuko proper'), not the separately coded neighbours Lopit (lopi1242), Dongotono (dong1294), Lokoya (loko1254) or Lango (lang1322).

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog (Coates 1985 p. 102): Otuho tonal, stress 'very indistinct', many words without a stressed syllable, tone the significant feature. Tucker & Bryan add, at Paranilotic-group level only, a placement norm (stress on the stem syllable, never Lotuho-specific) alongside a tone system and an explicit remark that tone vs stress dominance can be hard to determine. Compatible in type (tone language with weak/derivative stress); the stem-stress norm is extra detail not on record. Mild tension: Coates denies a consistent stressed syllable in many Otuho words, whereas T&B's group norm implies one; T&B give no Otuho evidence for it.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Group-level statement for the Paranilotic languages (Bari, Lotuho, Teso, Maasai, Kalenjin): stress normally falls on the stem syllable of a word; tone is treated separately (sec. 2a, Tone Classes); in Bari stress shifts significantly in certain (tone-class/emphatic) circumstances and the authors note it is sometimes hard to tell whether tone or stress is the dominant factor. No Lotuho-specific stress sentence exists in sec. 2b (probes for LOTUHO near 'stress' returned only unrelated passages).
new_statements.secondary_stress: nothing said in the recovered text
new_statements.exceptions: Bari only: 'significant shifting of stress in certain circumstances' (Tone Class 1 vs 2, emphatic forms) and cases where tone vs stress dominance is undetermined; 'See also under Gender, § 6'. Observation: tone and stress patterns 'may vary widely even between dialects' (Nandi vs Kipsigis example).
new_statements.identity_note: Tucker & Bryan's 'LOTUHO' = Otuho/Lotuko/Lotuxo (otuh1238), one of the five heads of their ch. 31 'Paranilotic' (= Nilo-Hamitic; today Eastern + Southern Nilotic): Bari (with Kakwa notes), Lotuho, Teso (with Karimojong/Turkana/Toposa notes), Maasai, Kalenjin (Pakot, Nandi/Kipsigis). The stress statement recovered is chapter-level; its illustrations are Bari (and Nandi/Kipsigis for dialect variation), none Lotuho. Coates 1985 describes Otuho as spoken around Torit (SIL/IRL orthography work).

readall_conflicts: No placement conflict. The catalog record (Coates 1985, Otuho-specific, verified) says Otuho is tonal with very indistinct stress and many words lacking a stressed syllable; Tucker & Bryan 1966 (recovered as scanned snippets, pp. 449-450) state for the Paranilotic group as a whole that 'Stress falls normally on the Stem syllable of words', treat tone separately (Tone Classes, sec. 2a), and concede that it is sometimes 'hard to determine whether tone or stress is the dominant factor' (Bari examples). The stem-stress norm is a group generalisation with no Lotuho data behind it in the recovered text, so it refines rather than contradicts the record; the only tension is that Coates denies a consistent stressed syllable in many Otuho words while T&B's norm presupposes one.

sources.note: Sec. 49 'Accento' p. 18: Lotuxo has accented syllables but accent 'non vi abbia quell'importanza che ha in altre lingue'; example ojó 'disse' vs ójo 'cioè'; warns not to mistake tone for accent, some words have no true accent, only tone ('modulazione'); tone not marked in the grammar. Sec. 433-437 (pp. 203-204) give morphology-specific accent positions in imperative forms (2sg affirmative penultimate, monosyllabic roots final, 3pl always final, 2pl affirmative no clear accent) and say tone is more important than accent. No general word-level rule.
